top_story: Iran’s coercive reach now spans prison cells at home and diaspora communities abroad: on 12 November, a UK court convicted two men for surveilling British-based journalists in an Iranian-linked plot, and by 13 November death-row prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani used an international rights award to publicly defy the state’s campaign of intimidation. In Gaza, the sharper and more immediate deterioration came later on 13 November, when intensified Israeli strikes killed 11 people, including in a hospital strike, as aid restrictions and falling temperatures left civilians exposed enough that a baby died of hypothermia. The pattern across both files is one of authorities and armed power pressing hardest where civilians are least protected, turning courts, prisons, borders, and even hospitals into sites of fear. The regional takeaway is that coercion is not only escalating through direct violence but also through the deliberate narrowing of civilian safety, whether by repression, transnational targeting, or siege conditions.
